quote: You perceive, of course, that this destroys the world.
content: The table describes a design nobody proposed: a utility that rewards desire strength times desire satisfaction, scored on future states of the programmer's mind. Preference-satisfaction proposals in welfare economics and in AI score outcomes by the principal's current preferences, not by preferences the agent can manufacture. Make that one change and the incentive to rewrite the programmer disappears. The example shows that one bad specification is bad. It has no bearing on the class of designs the essay goes on to dismiss.

quote: As a general rule, it is not possible to patch flawed FAI designs.
content: The rule is asserted twice and never argued, and the specific failure used to motivate it has since been analyzed and addressed. Using causal influence diagrams, Everitt et al. (2021) show that an agent which scores futures by its current reward function, rather than by the one it will later have, loses the incentive to tamper with that function. That is the incentive the table exhibits. Formal work on the off-switch game (Hadfield-Menell et al. 2017) derives an incentive to defer from the agent's uncertainty about its objective. Those results have their own limits. But "you cannot patch this" is exactly the kind of universal, non-empirical engineering claim the book warns against in others.

quote: If you try to make it so that the AI can’t modify the programmer, then the AI can’t talk to the programmer (talking to someone modifies them).
content: This is a false dichotomy. Ethics and law routinely distinguish informing someone from manipulating them, and recent work formalizes the difference in terms of incentives. On that account, manipulation is influence a system is incentivized to exert because it changes a person's beliefs or preferences in ways that serve the system's objective, bypassing the person's reasons (Carroll et al. 2023). The distinction is hard to operationalize, but "all talking is modification" treats a hard problem as an impossible one.

quote: “I should X” means that X answers the question, “What will save my people? How can we all have more fun? How can we get more control over our own lives? What’s the funniest jokes we can tell? …”
content: This is analytic descriptivism with the reference held fixed, close to Frank Jackson's moral functionalism (From Metaphysics to Ethics, 1998; book, no DOI), and it faces that view's best-known objection. Horgan & Timmons (1992) imagine a Moral Twin Earth whose moral terms are governed by a different fixed question. Intuitively the two communities disagree about what is right; on this semantics they are simply talking about different things. Toby Ord's summary wasn't a misunderstanding so much as a report that the view seems to collapse into relativism. The reply here redescribes the view without answering that worry.

quote: but I know, as all non-moral-relativists instinctively know, that the question surely is not just
content: The clinching step is an appeal to what non-relativists "instinctively know." But the view just stated makes the moral question whatever question human brains implement. The essay has also conceded that "moral arguments ... modify our terminal values, and even ... what we count as a moral argument." If argument can change the question, which version is the fixed one: today's, the one after a given argument, or the endpoint of some idealized extrapolation? The computation is "fixed" only once an idealization procedure is specified, and that unresolved problem passed straight to the later Coherent Extrapolated Volition proposal.
